title: Robinhood's CEO Asked Washington to Rebuild the Stock Market. Wall Street Just Answered With $12 Billion.
subtitle: Vlad Tenev spent the week pushing US regulators to green-light tokenized stocks — equities on blockchain rails that trade 24/7 and settle instantly. After a Bitcoin-fueled Friday added roughly $12 billion in market value, the market is clearly listening. The twist? The product already exists — just not for Americans.
summary: Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev spent the week publicly urging US regulators to set a framework for tokenized stocks — real equities on blockchain rails that trade 24/7, settle instantly, and can be programmed. On Friday the market answered: shares surged double digits in their best day in weeks, adding roughly $12 billion in market value as Bitcoin broke out and the tokenization push caught fire. The irony is that Robinhood's own blockchain already offers about 190 tokenized US stocks across 120+ countries — just not to Americans. The tokenized-stock market is still tiny at roughly $2.5 billion worldwide, which makes Friday's pop a bet on a future that hasn't been legalized yet.

bodyHtml:
Here's a sentence you don't hear every day: the CEO of America's favorite trading app went to Washington this week and asked regulators to let him rebuild the stock market. Wall Street's answer landed Friday — shares surged double digits, notching the stock's best day in weeks and adding roughly $12 billion in market value. That's a lot of money to put behind an idea that isn't even legal in the US yet.

Quick refresher, because Robinhood is so ubiquitous it's easy to forget what it actually does. It's the app that turned phone-based, commission-free investing into the default way a generation trades — the place where millions of young Americans buy their first stock between sips of iced coffee, and the reason "zero commissions" stopped being a selling point and became table stakes. Love it or hate it, Robinhood didn't just ride the retail-trading wave; it built the surfboard.

Now Vlad Tenev wants to build the next wave. Since Tuesday, he's been publicly urging US regulators to lay out a framework for tokenized stocks — real equities represented as blockchain tokens that can trade around the clock, settle instantly, and be programmed like software. He calls it a global "tokenization supercycle." "We're at the beginning of a supercycle," he said, "and it's going to take over the entire financial system."

His pitch is part economics, part warning: if America won't write the rules, someone else will. "It would be a strange outcome if the rest of the world could build the future of ownership around American assets while Americans themselves were left behind," Tenev argued.

And here's the kicker — the product already exists. Robinhood Chain, the company's own blockchain, went live in July and already offers tokenized exposure to about 190 US stocks across more than 120 countries, backed 1:1 and trading 24/7. The catch: Americans can't touch it. The most futuristic product from an American company is walled off from its home market by US rules — you can trade a tokenized piece of an American stock from Singapore, just not from San Francisco. That irony is doing a lot of heavy lifting this week.

This matters way beyond one stock. Tokenization is a rebuild of the market's plumbing, not a gimmick. Settlement goes from days to seconds. The trading day stops being a 9-to-5 ritual and becomes a 24/7 utility. Ownership becomes programmable — exactly the kind of rail that AI-native trading and autonomous agents will eventually run on. Think of it this way: today's market runs on a schedule and a stack of middlemen; tokenized rails run on code, around the clock, everywhere at once. And Robinhood, with tens of millions of customers already in the app and a distribution engine most banks would kill for, is positioning itself as the on-ramp to all of it.

Then Friday happened. Bitcoin broke decisively higher in its best week since 2023, crypto-adjacent names ripped, and Robinhood — the stock that's become the market's favorite bridge between the crypto and equity worlds — surged 13.7%, its best day in weeks and the top gainer in the S&P 500. The two stories, a Bitcoin breakout and a regulatory push, fed each other, and Robinhood sits right where they intersect. It didn't hurt that the week opened with a White House meeting where crypto executives pressed Congress on the Clarity Act, the stalled digital-asset bill that could clear the runway for exactly the products Tenev is describing.

One honest caveat before you get carried away: the entire tokenized-stock market is still tiny — roughly $2.5 billion worldwide. Friday's pop wasn't the market pricing in today's revenue; it was pricing in a future that hasn't been legalized yet, and the legislative path is real but far from guaranteed.

But that's the fun of being early. Robinhood isn't begging Washington for a handout — it's asking permission to build the next era of markets, and it's running the technology overseas while the debate drags on at home. When the most popular trading app in America is the one arguing for a 24/7, programmable stock market, that's not a press release. That's a road map. And on Friday, Wall Street put roughly $12 billion behind it.
